A.explanation: 2200 N is too small because it underestimates the clockwise moment of the 4000 N bridge weight and 600 N man about support Y.

B.explanation: 2300 N results from an error in the moment distances, such as not using 8 m for the 600 N man from support Y.

C.explanation: Taking moments about Y gives $F_X \times 12 = 4000 \times 6 + 600 \times 8$, so $F_X = 2400 \text{ N}$.

D.explanation: 2600 N is too large and would give a larger anticlockwise moment about Y than the total clockwise moment from the weights.

hints: Notice the bridge is uniform and 12 m long, so its 4000 N weight acts at the centre, 6 m from each support.
For equilibrium the sum of moments about any point is zero, so take moments about support Y to leave only the unknown force at X in the equation.
Write $F_X \times 12$ equal to $4000 \times 6$ plus $600 \times 8$, where 8 m is the distance of the man from support Y, then solve for $F_X$ in $\text{N}$.
walkthrough: The bridge is uniform, so its 4000 N weight acts at its midpoint, 6 m from support X and 6 m from support Y.
The man of weight 600 N is 4 m from X, so he is $12 - 4 = 8 \text{ m}$ from Y.
For equilibrium, the resultant moment about any point is zero. Take moments about Y so the unknown force at Y has zero moment.
Anticlockwise moment from X equals sum of clockwise moments: $F_X \times 12 = 4000 \times 6 + 600 \times 8$.
Calculate the right side: $4000 \times 6 = 24000 \text{ N m}$ and $600 \times 8 = 4800 \text{ N m}$, giving total $28800 \text{ N m}$.
Hence $F_X = 28800 / 12 = 2400 \text{ N}$ upward, with correct force units. This is option C.
